_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: And yet for uncertainty etc. it does not teach: in the latter clause, concerning misuse [of consecrated property].
rashi:a1.2: Whose is this: that is, whose is the first tanna [of the baraita]?
rashi:a1.3: Rabbi Akiva deems one liable for uncertain misuse etc.: in the chapter Dam Sheḥita (below, Keritot 22a).
rashi:a2.1: And it teaches: during five lapses of awareness etc.: it is lapses of awareness that differentiate, but not offerings. And conclude from it that Rabbi Yehoshua retracted.
rashi:a4.1: Rather, what is there for you to say, that the baraita is a dispute of tanna’im? [This is said] in astonishment. That is: what do you want to understand from this baraita? That it is a dispute of tanna’im: the first tanna, who teaches “lapses of awareness,” implying that lapses differentiate and not offerings, holds that Rabbi Yehoshua accepted it and retracted; and the one who teaches “five offerings during one lapse of awareness, he is liable for each one” is another tanna, who holds that he did not accept it? Even this you have not established from it, that it is a dispute of tanna’im, for you may even say it is Rabbi Akiva, and the first tanna follows Rabbi Akiva, since he teaches “lapses,” implying lapses and not offerings. And as for what troubles you, that it does not teach a provisional guilt offering for uncertain misuse —
rashi:a5.1: This tanna holds like him etc.: and the one who teaches “from five offerings during one lapse of awareness he is liable for each one” is another tanna, and it is Rabbi Yehoshua.
rashi:a6.1: Five items in a burnt offering combine: with regard to an olive-bulk for offering them up outside [the Temple], for if he offered them up he is liable to karet. And that is why it mentions a burnt offering, since in other offerings the meat does not combine, because they are not burnt whole. “Like that which we learned” etc.: here too, he ate from these five items.
rashi:a7.1: In the shoulder: there are five limbs [in it]: the hoof, and the lower bone up to the knee joint, and two bones, apart from the shoulder [itself].
rashi:a7.2: Five kinds of pot dishes: for example leeks, onions, cabbage, gourd and turnip, and he ate [meat cooked] with this one by itself and with that one by itself.
rashi:a7.3: Five kinds of flavors: roasted, cooked, pickled, well-boiled, and pot-roasted.
rashi:a8.1: Mishna: Many labors of the type of one labor: many subcategories of one primary category, on many Shabbatot: those he performed on this Shabbat he performed on other Shabbatot, and all of them during one lapse of awareness. And in the Gemara it asks: What is his dilemma, that he mentions two things, many Shabbatot and many subcategories? And why does he mention subcategories and not primary categories?
rashi:a9.1: Many outcomes: many matters, as with Shabbat, where there are primary categories of labor and their subcategories.
rashi:a9.2: A menstruating woman, with whom there are not many outcomes: for the liability with her is only for intercourse, and he is liable for each act of intercourse during one lapse of awareness, as Rabbi Eliezer said above in the Gemara: he engaged in intercourse with her and again engaged in intercourse with her etc.
rashi:a10.1: And the menstruating woman is prohibited regarding him: as it is written: “And both of them shall be cut off from among their people” (Leviticus 20:18).
rashi:a11.1: With minor girls: like “with a minor girl”; and what are “minor girls”? Minor girls in general. That is: one who engages in intercourse many times with one of the minor girls during her menstruation will prove it, since she is not prohibited regarding him, and he is liable for each act of intercourse.
rashi:a13.1: One who copulates with an animal will prove it: that he is liable for each act, as we said above, the reason being that it is impossible to combine the acts.
rashi:a13.2: The animal is like Shabbat: this is a dispute in the Gemara. According to the one who says Rabbi Akiva accepted it from Rabbi Eliezer, this is what he said to him: the animal is like Shabbat; just as with an animal he is liable for each one, so too with Shabbat he is liable for each one, for he did not know how to reply at all. And according to the one who says he did not accept it from him, this is what he said to him: about the animal too I am uncertain, as with Shabbat.
rashi:a14.1: Gemara: What did he ask of him: that he mentions many Shabbatot, performing on this one the same labor he performed on that one, and mentions subcategories and not primary categories.
rashi:a14.2: If he was asking him whether Shabbatot are like separate entities or not: if this one, who on several Shabbatot performed on this one the same labors he performed on that one, during one lapse of awareness, without it becoming known to him in between: do we say that since he performed them on two Shabbatot, these two Shabbatot are like two separate bodies of transgression, as though he reaped and sowed during one lapse of awareness, where he is liable for each one; or not, but rather we say it is like one who performs one labor several times during one lapse of awareness, who is liable only once? If this is what he was uncertain about, why does he mention subcategories? Let him ask it this way: one who performs one primary labor on many Shabbatot, what is [the law]?
rashi:a15.1: If he was asking him about offshoots of labors: if one performs many subcategories of one primary category, whether he is liable one or for each one, and that is why he mentions subcategories. If so, why does he mention many Shabbatot? Let him ask it this way: one who performs many labors of the type of one labor on one Shabbat.
rashi:a16.1: He asked him two things: and he resolved both of them stringently, since it teaches “liable for each and every one,” even though from the menstruating woman he could resolve only one of them for him, since with a menstruating woman there are no subcategories.
rashi:a17.1: And Shabbatot, how: which of them? That is, what are the circumstances in which he performs this (primary) labor on several Shabbatot? With unwitting Shabbat and intentional labors, it is obvious to Rabbi Akiva that he is liable for each one, for we do not say it is one error; rather we say that the intervening days are awareness, as if it had become known to him in between that it was Shabbat, and it is like one who performs one labor during several lapses of awareness.
rashi:a18.1: And intentional Shabbat: he knows that it is Shabbat, and unwitting labors, thinking this labor is permitted: that is what he asked him. For here one cannot say that the intervening days are awareness to differentiate, because they serve as awareness for knowing that it was Shabbat, but with regard to being unwitting about labors there is no awareness until he learns. And this is what he was uncertain about: this one who performed one labor on two Shabbatot, do we say that since they are on two days, even though it is one lapse of awareness with regard to the labors, these Shabbatot are like separate bodies of labor that are not similar to one another, as when one sowed and reaped during one lapse of awareness with intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors, where he is liable for each one, as we say in Shabbat (70a): “One” that is “many”: intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors?
rashi:a18.2: Or not: [they are not] like separate bodies, and he has performed one labor ten times during one lapse of awareness, for which he is liable only once.
rashi:a19.1: Or perhaps, with intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors, it is obvious to him that Shabbatot are like separate bodies of labors that are not similar to one another, so that one who performs them unwitting about labors and intentional about Shabbat is liable twice, which is “one that is many”; and it is with unwitting Shabbat and intentional labors that he was uncertain. For even if we say they are like separate bodies, he would be liable only once, as that is “many that are one,” since one who performs two primary labors with unwitting Shabbat and intentional labors during one lapse of awareness is liable only once, unless there is awareness in between that it is Shabbat, which serves to differentiate, since lapses of awareness differentiate. And this is what he was uncertain about: do we say that the intervening days are awareness, like one who was made aware that it is Shabbat, or not?
tosafot:a2.1: Rather, isn’t it Rabbi Yehoshua, and it teaches: during five lapses of awareness he brings five sin offerings: because specifically lapses of awareness differentiate. And the Ri explains that the same applies: he could have cited the first clause, “five pieces from five pots from one offering, he is liable only one,” since in the mishna too he compares pots. But since pots were not the question, he did not cite it.
tosafot:a5.1: You may even say it is Rabbi Akiva: and “five offerings during one lapse of awareness, he is liable for each one” is not Rabbi Akiva but Rabbi Yehoshua.
tosafot:a7.1: In the shoulder of a burnt offering: it has seven bones.
tosafot:a7.2: In five kinds of pot dishes: the Ri explains, for example roasted, cooked, fried, pot-roasted and pickled; and five kinds of flavors, for example pepper, ginger, [aromatic] cane, cinnamon and cassia. And Rashi did not explain it so.
gershom:a1.1: [A mark in the printed text here reads: up to here belongs to daf 15b.] And yet for their uncertainty: of misuse, for uncertainty whether he ate from the five pots before the sprinkling of the blood, it does [not] teach that he brings a provisional guilt offering.
gershom:a2.1: Whose is this? The latter clause. If we say it is Rabbi Akiva, let it also teach in the latter clause etc.
gershom:a3.1: Rather, isn’t it Rabbi Yehoshua: the first clause of the baraita and the latter clause. And it teaches: during five lapses of awareness he brings five sin offerings; hence for five pieces from one offering in five pots during one lapse of awareness, he brings only one sin offering.
gershom:a4.1: Evidently Rabbi Yehoshua accepted this refutation from Rabbi Akiva, that he brings only one sin offering.
gershom:a5.1: Another version: since the first clause teaches that for five pieces from one offering during one lapse of awareness in five pots he is liable only one, evidently he does not derive notar from misuse. Conclude from it that he accepted it from him.
gershom:a6.1: Rather, on the contrary, from the latter clause: you can derive that he did not accept it from him, for it teaches that [from five] offerings he is liable for each one, because the bodies are differentiated; and the same applies that pots differentiate even in one offering. Evidently he derives notar from misuse. Conclude from it that he did not accept it from him.
gershom:a7.1: Rather, what is there for you to say? It is a dispute of tanna’im about this matter of Rabbi Yehoshua: there is a tanna who holds that he accepted it from him, and that tanna is Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon of our mishna; and there is a tanna who holds that he did not accept it from him, and that is the first tanna.
gershom:a8.1: And you may even say that all of it is Rabbi Akiva [Rabbeinu Gershom’s text reads “all of it”]: he did not say “all of it” strictly, since the clause “but if he ate five pieces” etc. cannot be established according to Rabbi Akiva, as we said. Rather he says “all of it” because both the first clause of the baraita and Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, follow Rabbi Akiva: from five offerings they bring for each one, whereas from one offering in five pots he brings only one; that too follows Rabbi Akiva.
gershom:a9.1: And this tanna of “but if he ate” is also Rabbi Akiva, except that he holds like him in one matter and disagrees with him in one matter.
gershom:a10.1: He holds like him in one matter: in lapses of awareness, that for notar from one offering in five pots he brings only one.
gershom:a11.1: And disagrees with him: on misuse and uncertain misuse, since he does not teach: “And for their uncertainty he brings a provisional guilt offering for each one.”
gershom:a12.1: What are the circumstances of five pots, such that when he ate them in five pots he is liable?
gershom:a13.1: Shmuel says: Like that which we learned: Five items in a burnt offering combine: the meat, the fat, the wine, the fine flour and the oil. The wine, the fine flour and the oil are the libations and the meal offering brought with the burnt offering. And since it was necessary to state that they combine to an olive-bulk for liability, conclude from it that each one is a separate pot, a food in its own right, so that if he ate an olive-bulk from each one he is liable five times. For if they were not five pots, there would be no need to say that they combine, since it would be obvious that they combine.
gershom:a14.1: Ḥizkiyya says: you may even say that in the burnt offering itself, without the wine, fine flour and oil, you find five pots: for example, he ate from five limbs of the burnt offering; it counts as five pots.
gershom:a15.1: Reish Lakish says: even in one limb you find five pots, in the shoulder, which has five bones: the first, the flat of the foreleg; the second, the shank bone above it; the third, the foreleg bone that is given to the priests; the fourth, the bone called “round,” which is on top of it; and the fifth, the shoulder blade.
gershom:a16.1: For example, he ate even one limb in five kinds of pot dishes: for example, part of it with leeks, part with cabbage, part with turnips, part with beets and part with legumes.
gershom:a17.1: In five kinds of flavors: for example roasted, cooked, well-boiled, seasoned and fried.
gershom:a18.1: One who performs many labors on many Shabbatot of the type of one labor: that is, for example, a primary category and its subcategories, or he did subcategories of one primary labor; that is “of the type of one labor.”
gershom:a19.1: And just as a menstruating woman, who has not etc.: that is, if with a menstruating woman, who has not many outcomes for many sin offerings, meaning she has not many matters like the primary labors to make him liable to many sin offerings, and has no subcategories, but only the liability for intercourse, and even so he is liable for each act of intercourse; then Shabbat, which has many outcomes for sin offerings, such as the thirty-nine primary labors and subcategories without number, [is it not right that he be liable for each one]?
gershom:a20.1: Would you say the same of Shabbat, which has only one prohibition: that he is prohibited regarding Shabbat alone, but Shabbat is not prohibited regarding him.
gershom:a21.1: (He said to him: One who engages in intercourse with minor girls who are menstruating will prove it, as there is only one prohibition: that he is prohibited regarding them, and they are not, since they are still minors, alone; and Shabbat is not prohibited regarding him.) [The printed text sets this line in parentheses; the next note gives it in full.]
gershom:a22.1: He said to him: One who engages in intercourse with minor girls who are menstruating will prove it, as there is only one prohibition with them: he is prohibited regarding them, but they are not prohibited regarding him, since they are still minors and not subject to prohibitions. And even so he is liable for each one.
gershom:a23.1: Although they have no prohibition now, they have one after time: when they are grown, they have two prohibitions. Would you say the same of Shabbat etc.
gershom:a24.1: One who copulates with an animal will prove it: as there is only one prohibition, for he is prohibited regarding the animal but the animal is not prohibited; and even so he is liable for each act. So too I will bring [the same reasoning to] Shabbat.
gershom:a25.1: I said to him: The animal is like Shabbat. That is: about the animal, where he has only one prohibition, I am also uncertain, as with Shabbat, whether he is liable once for many acts or for each one.
gershom:a26.1: What was Rabbi Akiva uncertain about? Whether many Shabbatot are like the differentiated bodies of menstruating women, so as to make him liable for each Shabbat, just as one who engages in intercourse with many menstruating women is liable for each one.
gershom:a27.1: If so, let him ask him about one who performs one labor on many Shabbatot, similar to the menstruating woman, since it is one labor.
gershom:a28.1: Whether offshoots of labors are like labors, so as to make him liable for them as for primary labors, or not, is what he asked him, and that is why he said “of the type of one labor.” If so, let him ask him about one who performs many labors, subcategories of the type of one labor, on one Shabbat. Why does he say “on many Shabbatot”?
gershom:a29.1: He asked him two things, and here they explain his question: one who performs one labor on many Shabbatot, that is, whether they are like separate bodies; and one who performs many labors of the type of one labor even on one Shabbat during one lapse of awareness, that is, whether offshoots of labors are like labors.
gershom:a30.1: [A mark in the printed text here reads: up to here belongs to daf 16a.] And he resolved for him that Shabbatot are like bodies, from the menstruating woman: if with one menstruating woman he is liable for each act of intercourse, all the more so with acts of intercourse with many menstruating women, whose bodies are differentiated, he is liable for each one. So too Shabbatot are like bodies.
gershom:a31.1: And he resolved for him that offshoots of labors are like labors: since he said “And just as a menstruating woman, who has not many outcomes,” it follows that had she many outcomes he would be liable for each kind. So too with Shabbat, which has subcategories, let him be liable for a subcategory as for a primary labor.
rashi:b1.1: It stands to reason: from the mishna that we cite below.
rashi:b3.1: Who forgets the essence of Shabbat: who thinks Shabbat was not written in the Torah; that is, unawareness of both this and that is in his hand, unwitting about Shabbat and unwitting about labors.
rashi:b3.2: One sin offering: for all of them, since it is a single error. And there one cannot say that the intervening days are awareness, for he never knows the essence of Shabbat until he learns.
rashi:b4.1: Who knows the essence of Shabbat: who knew that the forty [less one] primary labors are prohibited on Shabbat, but does not know that today is Shabbat; that is, unwitting about Shabbat and intentional about labors. And he performed many labors on many Shabbatot, and it did not become known to him in between that he had sinned.
rashi:b4.2: He is liable for each and every Shabbat: one sin offering, because the intervening days are awareness with respect to being unwitting about Shabbat. And he is not liable for each labor of each Shabbat, since it is unwitting about Shabbat and intentional about labors, which is “many that are one.” But one cannot say [the text adds in parentheses: “they resolved from it”] that Shabbatot are like separate entities, so that we would say that is why he is liable for each Shabbat; for perforce [Rabba] goes on to infer from the last clause that this tanna does not hold that Shabbatot are like separate entities, and the reason for the first clause is that the intervening days are awareness to differentiate.
rashi:b4.3: One who knows that it is Shabbat and performed [many] labors on many Shabbatot: and those he performed on this one he performed on that one, for he erred about many labors, thinking this labor is permitted. He is liable for each labor on the first Shabbat; that is “one that is many”: intentional about Shabbat and unwitting about labors.
rashi:b5.1: But “liable for each labor on each and every Shabbat” it does not teach: in this last clause, about intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors. Since the very same labors he performed on this one he performed on that one, and during one lapse of awareness, evidently Shabbatot are not like separate entities, and he is like one who performs one labor several times during one lapse of awareness, who is liable only once.
rashi:b6.1: Of the type of one labor, he is liable only one: since there is one primary category for all of them.
rashi:b7.1: And learn from it: from the middle clause, that with unwitting Shabbat and intentional labors it is obvious to Rabbi Akiva that the intervening days are awareness, since it teaches: “Liable for each and every Shabbat.”
rashi:b8.1: And he accepted neither of them from him: since it does not teach “liable for each primary labor of each Shabbat”; and the subcategories of labors he also did not accept from him, as the last clause teaches: “[of the type of] one labor” etc.
rashi:b9.1: Abaye said to him [etc.]: Not like separate entities: since it does not teach “for each labor of each Shabbat.”
rashi:b10.1: And he accepted it from him: since the middle clause teaches “liable for each and every Shabbat.” And this is what the last clause of the mishna means: “The animal is like Shabbat”: the law is with you, for certainly as with this, so with that.
rashi:b10.2: But he did not accept it from him: since the last clause teaches “of the type of one labor” etc. Between Abaye and Rabba there is a dispute about Rabbi Eliezer’s view on intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors: according to Rabba, Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable twice, and according to Abaye, even Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable only once. Furthermore, what Rabba says Rabbi Akiva was uncertain about, Abaye says was obvious to him. But both agree that according to Rabbi Akiva Shabbatot are not like separate entities, and that with unwitting Shabbat he holds the intervening days are awareness to differentiate.
rashi:b11.1: Rav Ḥisda says: With intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors, even Rabbi Akiva holds they are like separate entities: and what is taught in the “significant principle” about unwitting labors, “one who knows that it is Shabbat” etc., means he is liable for each labor of each and every Shabbat. Even though what he performed on this one he performed on that one, and during one lapse of awareness, he is nonetheless liable, since Shabbatot are like separate entities; that is why it teaches “on many Shabbatot.”
rashi:b12.1: And he accepted it from him: as the middle clause teaches: “One who knows the essence of Shabbat” etc.
rashi:b13.1: But he did not accept it from him: as the last clause teaches: “Of the type of one labor” etc.
rashi:b14.1: From where [do I say it]: that Rabbi Akiva holds that Shabbatot are like separate entities.
rashi:b14.2: Rabban Gamliel deems him liable: for there is no awareness for a half-measure, and the awareness in between does not serve to differentiate so that they would not combine.
rashi:b15.1: It enters your mind that Rabban Gamliel holds like Rabbi Akiva: as is explained below, that one cannot say he holds like Rabbi Eliezer, since it teaches “and [Rabban Gamliel] concedes.”
rashi:b16.1: And that which is taught “exempt” is with intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors: for since Shabbatot are like separate entities with intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors, it is like one who performs two half-labors that are not similar to each other during one lapse of awareness, who is exempt for all of them.
tosafot:b3.1: Rabba said: It stands to reason etc., and he resolved for him that Shabbatot are like separate entities etc. And if you will say: on the contrary, there is a difficulty from Rabba himself, for Rabba said earlier that according to Rabbi Eliezer one who reaped and reaped again is liable twice even on one Shabbat. If so, why does he need Shabbatot to be like separate entities? And likewise with the menstruating woman, what does he gain from differentiated bodies, since Rabbi Eliezer deems one liable for each act of intercourse? One can say that Rabbi Eliezer answered Rabbi Akiva according to Rabbi Akiva’s own view.
tosafot:b3.2: As we learned: A significant principle etc.… Rather, it is obvious that it is Rabbi Akiva, and conclude from it that the intervening days etc. And if you will say: what is so obvious to him, that he brings a proof from its words? One can say that Rabba held: since [Rabbi Akiva] is uncertain about subcategories of labors, which is “one who performs many labors of the type of one labor,” he is [also] uncertain about the clause adjacent to it, which is “one who knows that it is Shabbat and performed many labors” etc., that is, intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors, whether Shabbatot are like separate entities or not.
tosafot:b11.1: Rav Ḥisda says etc., and he resolved for him that the intervening days are awareness to differentiate etc.: when he brings a proof from him, it is not from the a fortiori inference, since Rabbi Akiva refuted the a fortiori inference, but from a received tradition that he is liable for each one.
tosafot:b14.1: Rav Ḥisda said: From where do I say it? As it is taught: One who writes etc. And Rabban Gamliel concedes that if he wrote etc. he is exempt. From this alone we would not prove that Shabbatot are like separate entities, from seeing that he is exempt, since one could say it deals with unwitting Shabbat and intentional labors, and that is why he is exempt: because the intervening days are awareness to differentiate. Even though Rabban Gamliel says there is no awareness for a half-measure, perhaps awareness like that does differentiate, since one can distinguish between [ordinary] awareness and the intervening days, and with the intervening days he concedes that the two do not combine. That is why he must bring another [baraita]: that with intentional Shabbat the Shabbatot have more significance, to be like separate entities, than with unwitting Shabbat.
tosafot:b15.1: And another baraita teaches etc.: That which is taught “exempt” is with intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors: since Shabbatot are like separate entities with intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors, it is like one who performs two half-labors that are not similar to each other during one lapse of awareness, who is exempt for all of them.
gershom:b1.1: And Shabbat, how was he uncertain? That is, whether with unwitting Shabbat and intentional labors, or with intentional Shabbat and unwitting labor. If unwitting Shabbat and intentional labors, where he is liable not for all the labors of each Shabbat but only once, since the labors were intentional,
gershom:b2.1: it is obvious to him that the weekdays in between, between each Shabbat, are awareness to differentiate for sin offerings, even though they are during one lapse of awareness.
gershom:b3.1: But intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors: that is, during one lapse of awareness,
gershom:b4.1: and he asked him whether Shabbatot are like bodies, so as to differentiate and make him liable for each Shabbat and for each primary labor, since unawareness of the labors is in his hand, or not.
gershom:b5.1: Or perhaps with intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors it is obvious to Rabbi Akiva that Shabbatot are like bodies: since there is a differentiation of sin offerings and labors, for with unwitting labors he is liable for each labor, so too there is a differentiation of Shabbatot, and they are like bodies, and he is liable for each Shabbat.
gershom:b6.1: And with unwitting Shabbat and intentional labors, since he is liable only once for all the labors, that is what he asked him: since he was unwitting about many Shabbatot during one lapse of awareness, are the days in between, between one Shabbat and the next, awareness to differentiate or not? Rava said [so Rabbeinu Gershom; the daf reads Rabba]: It stands to reason that unwitting Shabbat etc.
gershom:b7.1: [A footnote in the printed edition: In our Gemara the reading is Rabba; see Tosafot, s.v. “Amar Rabba”; according to our master’s reading, Rava, it is resolved.] Rava: From where do I say it? That with intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors he asked him whether they are like bodies, and he resolved for him that they are like bodies, so that he is liable for each Shabbat, and Rabbi Akiva did not accept it from him. And he also resolved for him that offshoots of labors are like labors, so that he is liable for each one, and he did not accept it from him.
gershom:b8.1: As we learned: A significant principle they stated with regard to Shabbat: Anyone who forgets the essence of Shabbat: for example, a child taken captive among the gentiles, who never knew of Shabbat at all,
gershom:b9.1: is liable only one sin offering when it becomes known to him, since unawareness of both this and that is in his hand.
gershom:b10.1: One who knows the essence of Shabbat: who knows that he was commanded about Shabbat but does not know that today is Shabbat, and performed many labors on many Shabbatot; he did not know that it was Shabbat but knew that these labors are prohibited on Shabbat, which is unwitting Shabbat and intentional labors. He is liable for each Shabbat only, and not for each labor, because it is obvious to him that with unwitting Shabbatot the days in between are awareness to differentiate. And one who knows that today is Shabbat, which is intentional Shabbat, and performed many labors on many Shabbatot during one lapse of awareness, unwitting about the labors, is liable for each primary labor.
gershom:b11.1: But “liable for each primary labor of each and every Shabbat” it does not teach.
gershom:b12.1: Whose is this mishna of the “significant principle”? And if you say it is Rabbi Eliezer, who says in the mishna “liable for each and every one,”
gershom:b13.1: say the last clause of the mishna of the “significant principle”: One who performs many labors of the type of one labor, that is, a subcategory and a primary category, is liable only one sin offering.
gershom:b14.1: And if it is Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Eliezer deems one liable for offshoots of labors as for labors, as he said above. Rather, it is obvious that this mishna is Rabbi Akiva.
gershom:b15.1: And conclude from it that with unwitting Shabbat and intentional labors it is obvious to Rabbi Akiva that the days in between are awareness to differentiate; and that is why he rules and teaches: “One who knows the essence of Shabbat and performed many labors on many Shabbatot is liable for each and every Shabbat.”
gershom:b16.1: And intentional Shabbat and unwitting labor is what he asked him, whether they are like bodies, so as to make him liable for each Shabbat.
gershom:b17.1: And he resolved it for him, as we see in the mishna that he said to him he is liable for each one. And he did not accept it from him, since we see that it is not ruled in the mishna of the “significant principle”: “liable for each primary labor of each and every Shabbat,” which would make him liable for each Shabbat, it does not teach. Evidently he did not accept from him that Shabbatot are like bodies. And he asked him about offshoots of labors, whether they are like labors, and he resolved that they are like labors, as we said above, and he accepted neither of them. Abaye said to Rava [so Rabbeinu Gershom; the daf reads Rabba]: Say the reverse: say that with intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors it is obvious to Rabbi Akiva that Shabbat is not like bodies, since it does not teach “liable for each primary labor of each and every Shabbat.”
gershom:b18.1: And unwitting Shabbat and intentional labor is what he asked him: are the days in between awareness to differentiate or not? And he resolved it for him from the menstruating woman: that when he is unwitting about the menstruating woman and intentional about the acts, the seven days of menstruation are awareness to differentiate, as is said below at the end of this discussion.
gershom:b19.1: And Rabbi Akiva accepted it from him, and that is why he ruled it in the mishna of the “significant principle”: one who knows the essence of Shabbat, which is unwitting Shabbat and intentional labor, and said that he is liable for each and every Shabbat.
gershom:b20.1: And he resolved for him that offshoots of labor etc., and he did not accept it from him, as he says in the last clause of the mishna: “The animal is like Shabbat.” Evidently he did not accept it.
gershom:b21.1: Rav Ḥisda says: With intentional Shabbat and unwitting labor, even Rabbi Akiva holds that they are like bodies. And if it is difficult for you: But “for each primary labor of each and every Shabbat” it does not teach! This is not difficult: since it teaches about intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors that he is liable for each primary labor, the same applies that he is liable for each and every Shabbat; and in fact he holds that they are like bodies. And when he asked him about unwitting Shabbat and intentional labors, whether the days in between are awareness to differentiate, he resolved for him that they are, and he accepted it from him and ruled it in his mishna.
gershom:b22.1: Rav Ḥisda said: From where do I say it, that even Rabbi Akiva holds that they are like bodies?
gershom:b23.1: As it is taught: One who writes two letters during one lapse of awareness is liable; during two lapses of awareness, that is, there was awareness in between,
gershom:b24.1: Rabban Gamliel deems him liable: as we explained earlier in this chapter, Rabban Gamliel holds there is no awareness for a half-measure. Even though there was awareness in between, the awareness does not interrupt the measure, and they combine, and he is liable.
gershom:b25.1: And the Rabbis exempt him: for they hold there is awareness for a half-measure, and it does not combine into the measure. It enters your mind that Rabban Gamliel holds like Rabbi Akiva, that Shabbatot are like bodies.
gershom:b26.1: Granted, according to me, who say [that with] intentional Shabbat [the text here reads “all of it”], Rabban Gamliel’s statement is reconciled with Rabban Gamliel’s: for it is taught “exempt” with intentional Shabbat and unwitting labors, since Shabbat is like bodies. And since they are like bodies, and he performed only half the measure of writing on this Shabbat and half on another Shabbat, therefore they do not combine and he is exempt. [A mark in the printed text here reads: up to here belongs to daf 16b.]
